text: Seventy-three minutes is barely long enough to teach a child to fish, which may be why the camera stays close to the hands doing it. Natan is five, his mother is taking him to Rome, and his father Jorge has the weeks before that departure to spend on the Chinchorro reef off the Mexican coast. Documentary and family drama at once, and the two labels do not fight: what is recorded is real and also arranged, a leave-taking organized as an apprenticeship in bait, boats and breath-holding. The Caribbean shallows are handled as a workplace rather than a view. Turquoise is unavoidable in water like that, but the attention goes under it, to the difference between looking at a reef and eating from one, and to a man showing a boy things he may not be there to watch him use.

A day and a night in Montevideo, and almost nothing in it that a plot would consider worth keeping. Three teenage boys move between errands, and the film declines to promote any errand into an event; character comes before narrative here, which in practice means jokes, dead time, and the specific boredom of young men with a whole city available and no money to spend in it. The scale stays small throughout: side streets, few interiors, ninety-four minutes of very little at length. Juan Pablo Rebella lets the comedy run dry and mostly at the boys' expense, without ever arranging their aimlessness into a lesson about aimlessness. What holds the thing together is timing — how long a scene waits before anyone speaks, and how seldom the wait resolves the way the setup has promised.

The job goes first, and then the day still has to be filled. Pablo Trapero stays with one middle-aged Argentine man after the work stops; the synopsis calls the film a portrait, and the word is exact, because no plot arrives to rescue him. What it follows is the arithmetic of looking: who would hire a man of his age to sit in a crane cab, how far he is willing to travel for a shift, what he can ask of people who knew him when he was earning. Ninety minutes, made in 2000, and the economics of that moment sit in the frame whether or not anyone in it says so. The register stays level rather than mournful. The real subject is how a man keeps being recognizable to himself while the thing that identified him is quietly withdrawn.

The lift is offered before it is asked for, which is the first thing to worry about. Durga and Kabeer leave their village at midnight for the railway station, and the highway supplies a vehicle, the men inside it, and a conversation that keeps returning to who she is and where she is really going. Sanal Kumar Sasidharan runs eighty-five Malayalam minutes mostly in the dark and mostly in motion, while the same night elsewhere is given over to a temple festival where devotees put their bodies through ordeals for the goddess whose name the woman carries. The film cuts between them and explains nothing. Nothing supernatural is needed to make the road the more frightening of the two rites: courtesy from strangers, extended and extended past the point where refusing it is still an option.

A letter stays private only as long as everyone who handles it behaves. Xiao Dou is quiet, lives with his sister, and inherits a Beijing mail route from a man dismissed for reading other people's correspondence; within weeks he has the same habit, and then something well past a habit. He stops seeing friends. He starts to intervene. He Jianjun made this in 1995, and the surveillance it describes is domestic and homemade — one clerk with a bag and too much time, learning a neighbourhood from the inside of its envelopes and deciding, without telling anyone, to adjust it. The film is patient about how small the first transgressions look. It is also alert to the pleasure involved: less appetite for scandal than the relief of a shy man finding a way into other lives without being seen in them.

Tens of thousands of deaths across six weeks is a figure, and a figure is the one thing a film cannot show. Lu Chuan takes the capture of Nanjing by the Imperial Japanese Army in 1937 and has two hours and twelve minutes in which to solve that. The answer is scale: streets, rooms, queues, decisions made by soldiers and civilians who cannot see past the next hour. It was made in China in 2009 for an audience that knows the outline before the lights go down, so nothing rests on suspense and nearly everything rests on duration — how long an occupation takes to organize itself, and what is done in the meantime by people waiting to learn the new rules. War films usually promise a battle. This one watches a city being converted, block by block, into something administered.

She leaves in the morning, in the car, with no plan past the road out of town. In 1969 the American woman on that road is usually a passenger; here she is driving, newly pregnant, and unwilling to let the pregnancy answer the question of what the rest of her life is for. Francis Ford Coppola gives her a hundred and one minutes and no destination, which makes the film a run of encounters rather than a journey with a shape. The interest is in her refusal to be sympathetic on cue: nothing has been done to her that would explain the leaving, no cruelty is produced for the record, and she goes anyway. That is a hard thing to build a drama around, and it is why the film still reads as unfinished business rather than as a period piece.

Seven months of permit applications for one concert, and then the bus still has to get there. Mamo is an old Kurdish musician with a reputation, living in Iran, set on crossing into Iraqi Kurdistan with ten of his sons and a vehicle in poor health. The comedy is the comedy of borders: everything turns on documents, and documents turn on whoever happens to be holding them that morning. Partway along the party collects Hesho, a singer, which adds a second illegality, since an Iranian woman may not sing in public and certainly not among a busload of men. Bahman Ghobadi keeps the road long and the music rationed. Mamo has been seeing his own death at half moon and mentions it the way other men mention weather; nobody aboard rates the prophecy above the state of the road ahead.

Tonda and Monika have known each other since childhood, which is exactly the problem. The terms were set before either of them had a vote, and revising the terms now would mean admitting that the arrangement they live inside was chosen rather than inherited. Bohdan Sláma follows a year of that stalemate in a Czech town worn down by industry, along with the obligations and other attachments that keep the stalemate convenient. A hundred and two minutes, and no crisis imposed from outside. What distinguishes it is temperature: warmth extended to people who behave badly mostly out of tiredness, and a refusal to turn hardship into either misery or charm. The Czech Lion for best film went to a picture whose largest events are domestic and easy to miss on the way past.

Three years of secret work, paid out in instalments to a loan shark, and nobody in the house asks where the money is coming from. Sara saved her husband's life by borrowing badly on his behalf, and the film's clock starts long after that decision, in the ordinary upkeep of the lie: the hours, the payments, the careful handling of a man who believes himself the provider. Dariush Mehrjui made it in Iran in 1993, and what tightens it is not danger so much as standing — how little of what she has done she is in any position to claim. A hundred and two minutes, largely indoors, the temperature rising a degree at a time. The suspense is not financial. It concerns how much of a wife's competence a marriage can survive being told about.

Ainara is seventeen, close to her final exams at a Catholic secondary school, and has told her family she would rather spend a trial period in a convent than pick a university course. The argument that follows is the film, not the vocation: her father moved by it, half-flattered, inclined to treat the choice as a gift; her aunt Maite convinced that a girl this able does not renounce the world unless something elsewhere has gone wrong. Alauda Ruiz de Azúa takes a hundred and twelve minutes and declines to adjudicate. The Golden Shell went to a Spanish film that keeps both readings load-bearing at once — belief as a decision an intelligent person can make and defend, and belief as a symptom the adults around her would rather diagnose than sit still and hear out.
